headline: A refusal that invites a retry no longer consumes what the retry needs, a route error no longer writes the credential out of the URL into the log and the audit chain, and a streamed upload to S3 no longer costs the memory of the whole object
summary:
Three classes of defect, each found to span more code than the first instance showed.

A transient refusal asks the caller to try again, and three paths had already spent something the second attempt needed: the vault passphrase was stripped from the environment before the derivation ran, a refused `b.localDb.thin` open left its file handle locked, and a refused restore left the destination directory it had just created. Each is fixed where the thing is consumed rather than where the error surfaced, so the retry the refusal invites now works. The same sweep found a vault rotation deriving its new wrapping key only after the staging directory was filled, so a busy derivation gate made a key rotation refuse its own retry.

`b.router` decided a log line's level from whether the status was 5xx-or-absent rather than from whether the refusal was deliberate, and built the line from `req.url`. A framework capacity refusal was therefore logged as an error with a stack that explains nothing, and a capability sitting in a path segment or a query string was written out. Eight sites recorded the raw URL, three of them into the signed audit chain, where it cannot be redacted afterwards; all eight now record the route.

A `put()` handed a stream read every part into memory before it initiated the upload, so streaming cost the same peak as a Buffer. It now initiates first and uploads a part at a time, with at most `partConcurrency` resident.

Alongside those: the Argon2id concurrency gate is documented as what it is, per-thread, and can now be shared across threads on request; `b.auth.password.exceedsCostCeiling` separates a hash this process cannot check from a wrong password; and a gate that compares what a primitive accepts against what its block documents now follows a block to an implementation in another module, which surfaced twenty-eight more options to write down.

items.title: b.auth.password.exceedsCostCeiling separates a hash this process cannot check from a wrong password
items.body: `verify` answers `false` for a wrong password and for a stored hash whose Argon2id cost is above the ceiling `costCeiling` holds, which it will not spend the work to check, and `needsRehash` does not separate them either. An application therefore had no way to tell a failed sign-in from a credential nobody can use until the ceiling is raised or the password is reset, and counted the second against its lockout policy. `b.auth.password.exceedsCostCeiling(stored)` answers that question from the stored string and the current ceiling, with no derivation, so it is safe on a login path. A string it cannot decode returns `false`, since nothing in it asks for any cost.

items.title: An Argon2id gate can be shared across worker threads
items.body: `b.auth.password.gate(n, { shared: true })` allocates a permit count that every thread holding the handle draws from, and `b.auth.password.gateHandle()` returns that handle to pass to a `worker_threads` Worker through `workerData`. The Worker adopts it with `gate(null, { shared: handle })`. The framework cannot propagate it on the operator's behalf: a Worker has its own module registry and no ambient channel to find a buffer the parent allocated, so the handle has to be threaded through each Worker the application starts. The limit is fixed when the shared gate is created and a later `gate(n)` that disagrees with it is refused, because reporting a limit the permits do not enforce is a bound in name only. `maxQueued` and `waitTimeoutMs` stay per thread, since each thread queues its own waiters, and `stats()` reports `shared` plus the shared `available` count.

items.title: The Argon2id concurrency gate is documented as per-thread, which is what it has always been
items.body: `b.auth.password`'s description, `stats`, the README's password entry, the operator security checklist and `b.credentialHash`'s note all called the gate process-wide. It is module state, so every `worker_threads` Worker that loads the framework holds its own limit and its own counts: `gate(4)` on five threads admits twenty concurrent derivations, not four. All five now say per-thread, and the opt-in shared gate above is there for deployments that need one bound across all of them. Nothing about the single-threaded case changes.

items.title: b.session reports an option it does not accept as a SessionError
items.body: `purgeExpired`, `purgeStale` and `logout` checked their option names with the plain validator, which raises a bare `Error` carrying no code, while every other option failure in those same functions raises a `SessionError` with one. A caller filtering on `isSessionError` saw a mistyped option name escape with nothing to match on. All three now raise `session/bad-opt`, which both purge blocks document.

items.title: A declared view or row policy that names a backend is applied only to that backend
items.body: `b.db.declareView` and `b.db.declareRowPolicy` accept a `backend` option. It was recorded on the returned migration spec and read by nothing: the runner picks the backend, and the dialect check reads the runner's name, so a view declared for `reporting` applied silently against `analytics`. Applying a spec that names a backend against a different one now raises `declare-view/backend-mismatch` or `declare-row-policy/backend-mismatch`. A spec that names no backend is still the runner's to place.

items.title: Twenty-eight options a primitive accepts are written down, and one that nothing read is no longer accepted
items.body: `b.staticServe.create` documented fourteen of the thirty-one options it accepts; the seventeen missing ones include every bandwidth and concurrency bound, the idle timeout, the range ceiling, the retention and revocation hooks, the attachment and safe-render switches, and the `onServe` and `onError` callbacks with their payloads. `b.fileUpload.create` omitted the two reasons recorded on its safety-disabled audit events, and the SOAP logout-request builder on `b.auth.saml.sp` referred to a sibling primitive instead of naming its seven. All are documented. `b.keychain.retrieve` and `b.keychain.remove` accepted `password` through an allowlist shared with `store` and read it in neither, so they now refuse it.

items.title: The logged and audited request target on an error page is named route
items.body: `b.errorPage`'s log fields and audit metadata carried the request target under `url` and now carry it under `route`, because the value is the matched route rather than the URL as sent. Operators parsing that log line or that audit record by field name should read `route`.

items.title: SECURITY.md describes the SAML primitive the framework ships
items.body: The threat model listed SAML under what the framework does not defend against, said no SAML primitive shipped, and promised that support "when added" would bake a signed-bytes-equality contract into the gate. `b.auth.saml.sp` has shipped since 0.8.62 and already does exactly that, so an operator reading that section would route around a primitive built for the threat. The entry moves to what the framework defends against, naming the single-element-match on the Reference URI, the digest over the canonicalized referenced element, the refusal of a Response carrying more than one `<EncryptedAssertion>`, and the refusal of an unsupported canonicalization, signature algorithm, digest or transform. What remains operator territory is named separately: supplying and trusting the IdP signing certificate, and storing the `InResponseTo` / RelayState pre-image / nonce that give freshness and replay defense.

items.title: A transient refusal no longer consumes what its retry needs
items.body: `argon2/busy` is transient and `b.retry.isRetryable` accepts it, so the refusal invites another attempt. Three paths had already spent something that attempt needed. The vault and audit-signing passphrase sources read their environment variable with a strip, so by the time a busy derivation gate refused, the variable was gone and the retry reported no passphrase source at all; the resolved passphrase is now held for the retry and zeroed once the operation ends either way. `b.localDb.thin` left its SQLite handle open when a pragma or the schema SQL was refused, which locks the file on Windows, so the retry could not open it. `readBundle` created the destination directory before decrypting, so a wrong passphrase left an empty directory and the corrected retry refused with `backup/dest-exists`; it now decrypts first and claims the directory with a create whose `EEXIST` is the refusal, removing what it created if the extraction fails. The same sweep found `b.vaultRotate.rotate` deriving its new wrapping key only after the staging directory was built and filled, so a busy gate during a key rotation left a staging directory that made the retry refuse; the derivation now happens before anything is written.

items.title: A failed init releases the handle, descriptors and pools it had already taken
items.body: A teardown that opens with a check on an initialized flag releases nothing when init threw before that flag was set. `b.db.init` opens the SQLite handle and then runs eight further checks that can refuse, and its failure path released the plaintext working-copy claim but not the handle, while `close()` declined to release it too, so an operator had no way to close the file and the next attempt orphaned the descriptor. `b.logStream.init` builds its sinks one at a time, each opening a file descriptor, so a later sink's refused level left every earlier one open. `b.externalDb.init` builds a connection pool per backend, each arming a reaper, with five configuration refusals after the first pool exists. All three now release on the failure path, and their teardown releases what it can see rather than keying on the flag.

items.title: A route error is logged at a level that reflects whether the refusal was deliberate
items.body: The level came from the status being 5xx-or-absent, so a framework capacity refusal was written at error level with five stack frames that explain nothing, and a burst of them under load wrote one per request. A framework error that declares itself transient is now recorded at debug, any other framework error at warn, both without frames and both carrying the error's code; an error that is not a framework error keeps error level and its frames, which is the case the frames exist for. A 4xx refusal stays at debug as before.

items.title: A middleware failure writes one line, and it names the middleware
items.body: `router.use()`'s catch logged a line of its own and then rethrew, so the router's own error logging wrote a second line about the same failure, with the stack twice. The catch now attaches the middleware's name to the error, which is the only thing it knows that the logging does not, and the single line names it.

items.title: A pragma sent through the session store runs every step
items.body: `b.session.stores.localDbThin`'s `execute` sent anything that was not a `SELECT` or a `RETURNING` through a single statement step. `PRAGMA incremental_vacuum` frees one page per step, so a maintenance call through the store contract freed exactly one page whatever count it was handed, and reported the previous statement's change count as `rowCount`; measured on a 445-page freelist, `incremental_vacuum(1000)` freed 1 page and reported 4000. A pragma that answers with a value was unreadable for the same reason. The store now uses the same row-returning predicate `b.clusterStorage` already used, which classifies both correctly.

items.title: Raising a connection pool's max admits the callers already queued
items.body: `b.externalDb.configurePool(name, { max })` is how an operator relieves a pool that callers are queued on, and the queue was served only when a connection came back. The slack a resize created therefore reached nobody until one of the in-flight queries finished, which is the query the operator is waiting out: raising `max` from 1 to 4 behind a long-running statement left `listBackends()[0].pool` reporting `waiters: 1` with three connections' worth of room unused. A resize now admits whatever the new bound allows, the same way a release does.

items.title: A request target the URL parser refuses is answered with 400
items.body: `b.router`'s dispatch parsed the request target without guarding the parse, and `b.safeUrl` refuses a URL over 8 KiB. Node's own request-line limit is 16 KiB, so a target between the two reached the router and raised `safe-url/too-long` out of `handle` with no response written. It is now refused as `400 Bad Request: malformed request target`, like the other targets the router will not route. The router also derives that target in one place now, so the route named in a log line or an audit record is matched exactly as the request is dispatched: against the same canonicalized pathname and under the request's own method. A target differing only in its leading-slash run names the route it reaches rather than `(unrouted)`; one carrying an encoded separator names no route, since the request itself is refused; and a `POST /users/invite` registered after a `GET /users/:id` is no longer recorded as the latter.

items.title: The Argon2id gate holds its bound while a caller switches gates
items.body: `b.auth.password.gate(n, { shared })` may be called while derivations are running, and a derivation that outlives the call finishes on the gate that admitted it. Both of the gate's per-thread numbers were held in two places and read in one. The derivations running on a thread are counted separately for its own gate and for a shared one, and admission read only the counter of the gate it was on, so a derivation that outlived the call counted for nothing: with both gates set to one permit, a second derivation started immediately and two Argon2id allocations stood at once on one thread. A thread configured for one 1 GiB derivation could hold two. The waiting callers are queued the same way, and `maxQueued` was likewise checked against one queue, so a switch admitted a third caller past a `maxQueued` of one. All three switch directions did both: a shared gate to the thread's own, the thread's own to a shared gate, and one shared handle to another. Admission now weighs every derivation running on the thread and every caller waiting on it, which is what `stats()` has always reported, so a call made across a switch waits for the earlier work or is refused as `argon2/busy`. A derivation already running finishes on the gate that admitted it, which is why its release is bound to that gate, but a caller still queued has no such tie: it is handed to the gate the thread switched to, keeping the deadline it started waiting under rather than restarting `waitTimeoutMs`. Left behind, it waited on permits the thread no longer used, and would have run outside the bound of the gate the thread had moved to. Nothing changes for a thread that does not switch gates.

items.title: A streamed upload to an S3-compatible store holds parts, not the object
items.body: `put()` handed a stream read every part into an array before it initiated the multipart upload, so streaming an object cost the same peak memory as passing it as a Buffer, which is the reason to stream it. The upload is now initiated first and the source is read a part at a time, with at most `partConcurrency` parts in flight plus the one being filled, and the reader waits for a slot rather than running ahead. Because the source is now read after the upload exists, every exit that is not a completed upload aborts it, including a source stream that fails partway; a part that fails interrupts the read rather than leaving it parked on a quiet source; a failure before or during initiation closes the source rather than leaving the descriptor open; and a source that cannot be opened at all fails the call rather than emitting an unhandled `error` with nothing attached. The 10,000-part ceiling is refused before anything is sent for a Buffer, and as the parts are produced for a stream.

items.title: A credential in a request path or query string no longer reaches the log or the audit chain
items.body: `req.url` carries whatever the client sent, including a reset or invite capability in a path segment and every query parameter. Eight sites recorded it: `b.router` built its refusal and error lines from it, its middleware catch logged it directly, and its three TLS 0-RTT audit records carried it, while `b.errorPage` put it in both its log fields and its audit metadata on every error render. `b.errorPage` now records `b.requestHelpers.resolveRoute`, which prefers the matched route pattern and otherwise strips the query. The router's five sites all run before a route has been matched, so `req.routePattern` is not set yet and stripping the query still leaves the capability in the path: they resolve the registered route from the router's own table instead, recording `(unrouted)` for a path no route claims and `(unresolved)` for one that cannot be decoded. The audit path is the one that could not be undone, because the chain is signed and append-only, so a capability written there stayed written. Treat any capability-bearing URL in logs or audit records retained from an affected version as disclosed, and rotate it.

items.title: A record field built from the raw request URL fails the pattern gate
items.body: A log line or audit record that names the request target and assigns it from `req.url` is refused in favor of `b.requestHelpers.resolveRoute`. Reading `req.url` to route, hash or parse a request is not recording it and does not match.

items.title: The options-contract gate follows a block to an implementation in another module
items.body: The gate that holds a primitive's accepted options equal to its documented ones found the function beside the block, in the same file. A block documented in one module and implemented in another was therefore never compared, and counted as unmeasurable, which reads as a clean verdict rather than a gap. It now resolves the export chain to the implementing module, reads an allowlist held in a module-level array and consulted in a key loop, and follows one level of delegation to a local validation helper. That reached sixteen more blocks and surfaced the twenty-eight undocumented options above. The gate reports what it measured on every run, so a verdict over a shrinking scan is visible.

items.title: Read route rather than url on b.errorPage's log fields and audit metadata
items.body: Both now carry the matched route under `route`. A dashboard or alert that reads the `url` field of those records needs the new name.

items.title: A view or row policy that names a backend must be applied to that backend
items.body: A spec carrying `backend` now refuses to apply against a different one. Keep per-backend specs in per-backend migration sets, or drop the option and let the runner place them.

items.title: An option b.session does not accept now arrives as a SessionError
items.body: `purgeExpired`, `purgeStale` and `logout` raise `session/bad-opt` where they previously raised a bare `Error`. A caller matching on the message rather than the code is unaffected; one filtering on error type now sees these alongside the primitive's other refusals.

items.title: The Argon2id gate bounds one thread unless a shared handle is threaded through
items.body: No behavior changed here, but the documented guarantee did. A deployment running derivations in `worker_threads` Workers and relying on `gate(n)` for a process-wide bound was never getting one. Either accept the per-thread bound and size it accordingly, or create the gate with `shared: true` and pass `b.auth.password.gateHandle()` into each Worker.
